Dear Members of the Appeal Board, My name is Kevin Patteri, and my wife and I currently live in Harwood Farms. In advance of the upcoming meeting, I wanted to provide a brief outline of why we strongly support this variance and respectfully ask that the proposed development be allowed to move forward as presented. 1. Our Interest in the Development • We first learned about the proposed development behind Harwood Farms approximately five years ago. • It provides a rare opportunity to design and build our own custom home on a large lot within a subdivision setting in Pittsfield Township. • Our goal is to build our final home here and remain close to our friends, family, and community. 2. Why the Proposed Layout Appeals to Us • We believe the development has an attractive, low-density layout with large lots and substantial separation between homes. • It provides an alternative to the higher-density, builder-controlled developments common in the area. • The proposed layout allows homeowners to build custom homes while maintaining the character of a well-planned subdivision. 3. Lot 14 and the Setback/Frontage Issue • We are specifically interested in Lot 14, which is nearly 90,000 square feet, or approximately two acres. • Although it is the narrowest of the proposed lots, its overall size and depth provide ample room for appropriate driveway and mailbox placement, along with significant setbacks and separation from neighboring homes. • I have attached a rendering of our proposed house as it would look on an actual picture of lot #14. • We understand the purpose of the township's frontage and setback requirements, particularly on smaller lots. However, we believe those concerns have a substantially diƯerent impact when applied to lots of this size. • 4. Why We Believe a Variance Is Appropriate • I personally met with township staƯ to better understand the issue and appreciate the time they spent explaining the township's interpretation. • I understand that township staƯ have rules and ordinances they are responsible for applying. • At the same time, we believe the circumstances surrounding these unusually large cul-de-sac lots warrant individual consideration and are exactly why a variance should be approved. 5. Our Personal Investment • We have waited through months of delays due to an improper application and being unable to form a quorum. • We have now been waiting more than three years for the development to move forward. • My wife and I hope to make this our final home and continue calling Pittsfield Township home for many years to come. • It is critical that this variance is approved now, hopefully allowing some progress before the winter months puts the project on hold until the spring. 6. Our Request We recognize and respect the purpose of the township's setback and frontage requirements but we are simply asking the Board approve this variance after months of discussions and delays. We believe the proposed plan preserves the township's objectives while allowing an attractive, low-density development to move forward. Thank you for reviewing this information in advance of the meeting. I greatly appreciate your time and consideration and respectfully ask that you approve the appeal. Before allowing a variance to allow a wall sign exceeding the maximum square footage allowed in the Zoning Ordinance for Dental Associates, I respectfully wish to encourage the Zoning Board of Appeals to carefully consider the reasons for the variance. While I certainly don't want to impede the success of any business in our Township, I would hope that any variance to our ordinances be combined with thoughtful and compelling reasons, beyond simply to promote business. This would include deference to the original reasoning for the ordinance in the first place. I have often defended regulations by noting that nearly all regulations are intended to address the excesses of individuals and businesses to the detriment of the community. I do not believe that exceptions to the rules should be allowed unless it is clear that the exception benefits the community. I would hope that Dental Associates will provide evidence that their variance will benefit our community. If not, I do not see much reason to provide a variance. Thank you for your consideration. MOTION CARRIED 3.0 Communications and Announcements None 4.0 Items from the Floor None 5.0 Public Hearings 5.1 ZBA 26-05 Helmer Farms LLC – Submitted for Minimum Lot Width Interpretation. Benjamin Carlisle – Zoning Administrator presented ZBA 26-05 Helmer Farms LLC for minimum lot width interpretation. Helmer Farms LLC appeals the Zoning Administrator’s determination that the minimum lot width required in the RA-1 District must be measured at the minimum building line – the required minimum front-yard setback line – where that line intersects the side lot lines. The applicant instead contends that width may be measured farther into the parcel at the location selected for a proposed principal building. PITTSFIELD TOWNSHIP ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS Regular Meeting July 27, 2026 Page 2 of 9 Scope of the Appeal This appeal is limited to the meaning of the Ordinance definition of minimum lot width and whether the Zoning Administrator applied that definition correctly. The Board is not being asked to approve the proposed lots, grant a variance, or establish a separate standard for cul-de-sac lots. Those issues would require separate review under the applicable ordinance standards. Controlling Ordinance Language The applicant is requesting interpretation of Section 2.02 which states the following definition of minimum lot width: The straight-line distance between side lot lines, measured at the two points where the minimum building line, or setback, intersects the side lot lines. The Zoning Administrator’s interpretation is that minimum lot width must be measured at the required building line, defined as the line established by the minimum front yard setback. Member Krone asked the question if the board decided the Zoning Administrator errored in his interpretation of the ordinance and as mentioned the board’s decision would take precedence for future submittals would this mean the zoning code would have to change. Zoning Administrator Carlisle explained two ways this could be handled by the ZBA board: 1. The ZBA board would determine the Zoning Administration interpretation was in error and apply the same rational as the applicant used to determine future approvals. 2. The ZBA board felt the applicant and Zoning Administrator’s interpreted the ordinance incorrectly than the zoning ordinance would have to be amended to provide clarity of the definition. Member Krone asked if the board was allowed to consider alternative ways to interpret the current zoning code. Zoning Administrator Carlisle explained that the board cannot rewrite the zoning code but can interpret it differently than what’s being presented or determine I made an error in my interpretation, but the board is supposed to use the strict language of the code when making your determination. PITTSFIELD TOWNSHIP ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS Regular Meeting July 27, 2026 Page 3 of 9 The applicant Philip Conlin representing Helmer Farms LLC presented as follows: • Request that the ZBA board recognizes the R1-A zoning does in fact have two (2) distinct methods of measuring minimum lot width at the building line. • The appeal is necessary because the Township’s R1-A ordinance is silent on the method for measuring lot width on cul-de-sac lots. The Zoning Administrator applied the standard rectangular lot method of measuring minimum width to the cul-de-sac shaped lots. • Applying the rectangular method of measuring lot width on cul-de-sac is illogical. • It provides no practical purpose in maintaining one-acre rural lot sizes and in almost all existing R1-A zoned subdivisions in Pittsfield Township the rectangular measurement method was not used. • Requesting a relaxation of the Zoning Administrator’s decision of the rectangular lot measurement method for the cul-de-sac lots in this subdivision. • The applicant felt the ordinance was poorly written to address this situation. Chairperson Fisher asked the applicant where on the lot the measurement is being taken, as it differs from the location where the Zoning Administrator is taking the measurement. Philip Conlin on behalf of the applicant responded that the required 150-foot width can be met based on their lot configurations; however, it cannot be met when measured using the 50-foot measurement from the road right-of-way. Their intentions were not to try to insert the 150-foot width which felt is not needed for cul-de-sac lots. They also could not find another cul-de-sac lots within the township that would meet the requirement. They agreed with the Zoning Administrator’s interpretation of the ordinance but felt this would only work for regular shape lots and makes it difficult for irregular shape lots to meet this requirement. Member Haupt asked if the lots were zoned as two and a half (2 ½) acre minimal. The Zoning Administrator replied they were rezoned to one (1) acre lots. Chairperson Fisher opened the floor for public comments. Kevin Patteri who resides in Harwood Farms, expresses his support for the following reasons: • • Our goal is to design and build our final custom home on lot 14. We believe the development has an attractive, low-density layout with large lots and substantial separation between homes. PITTSFIELD TOWNSHIP ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS Regular Meeting July 27, 2026 Page 4 of 9 • • • • • It provides an alternative to the higher-density, builder-controlled developments common in the area. Although it is the narrowest of the proposed lots, its overall size and depth provide ample room for appropriate driveway and mailbox placement, along with significant setbacks and separation from neighboring homes. We believe the circumstances surrounding these unusually large cul-desac lots warrant individual consideration and are exactly why an appeal process exists. We believe the proposed plan preserves the township’s objectives while allowing an attractive, low-density development to move forward. If not approved, lot 14 could increase from approximately two acres to roughly four acres. We do not want a four-acre lot, and the additional acreage would significantly increase its cost and seem less consistent with a development where many lots are closer to one acre. Danny Szobo who resides off Warner Rd, commented as follows: • • As a builder would like the opportunity to build custom homes these lots. This is not uncommon for cul-de-sac properties in different municipalities to have the same problem where the front is very narrow. Jerry Helmer, who resides off Moon Road, asked whether the examples included in the packet would become nonconforming lots. Chairperson Fisher explained that the Township cannot change what was previously approved. However, if changes are made to an existing lot, it may then be considered a nonconforming lot. Motion by Member Wall, supported by Member Haupt, to close the Public Hearing ZBA 26-05 Helmer Farms, LLC Minimum lot width interpretation. Draft Data Center Zoning Ordinance Amendments NEW BUSINESS 1. 10774 Dixie Hwy Rezoning Application – 07-03-126-011 COMMUNICATION - Levy Updates and Project Status PUBLIC COMMENT Public Comment is the time for audience members to comment on items not on the agenda. This is not a question-answer period. Please keep comments to no more than three minutes. Comments may be submitted in advance of the meeting to the Township Clerk at clerk@springfield-twp.us or 248-846-6510. ADJOURNMENT Next Meeting: October 27, 2026 Regular Meeting 7:00 p.m. 12000 DAVISBURG ROAD l DAVISBURG l MICHIGAN l 48350 l 248-846-6500 l WWW.SPRINGFIELD-TWP.US Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING August 25, 2026 Call to Order: Chairperson Galley called the August 25, 2026 Regular Meeting of the Springfield Township Planning Commission to order at 7:00 p.m. at the Springfield Township Civic Center, 12000 Davisburg Rd., Davisburg, MI 48350. Prior to the meeting being called to order, Township Clerk Sean Miller addressed the Commission and public regarding a previous statement he had made on social media concerning data centers in Springfield Township. Clerk Miller clarified that while the Township had not received a formal data center application, there had been a pre-application meeting regarding a potential data center development on December 15, 2025. Clerk Miller accepted full responsibility for the incomplete statement, apologized for any confusion it caused, and stated that he would provide more accurate and complete information in future communications. He further noted that the Township Board had acted decisively in adopting a moratorium to study and revise the Township’s zoning standards for data centers. A member of the public interrupted to ask why the Pledge of Allegiance had not been said. The public stood and the Pledge was recited. Commissioners In Attendance: Brian Galley, Chair Andrew Donato Ruth Ann Hines Steve Felix Jason Price Kevin Sclesky Commissioners Absent: Mark Yovich Consultants’ Present: Megan Masson-Minock, Township Planner Jason Mayer, Township Engineer Approval of Agenda: Commissioner Hines moved to approve the agenda as written. Commissioner Felix supported. Vote. Yes: Galley, Hines, Sclesky, Felix, Donato, Price, No: None. Absent: Yovich. Motion approved. Approval of Consent Agenda: 1) Approve Minutes of July 28, 2026 Regular Meeting 1 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING August 25, 2026 Commissioner Hines moved to approve the agenda with the following changes: Under Heather Highlands, remove Chair Galley from the vote due to his recusal and add Commissioner Sclesky as the supporter of the motion. Commissioner Felix supported. Vote. Yes: Galley, Hines, Sclesky, Felix, Donato, Price, No: None. Absent: Yovich. Motion approved. Chairperson Galley acknowledged the large attendance and asked how many people were present because of information concerning a data center. Most hands went up. He stated that there was no datacenter application on the table in Springfield Township and noted that internet and social media information stating otherwise as incorrect. He said the Township had received one December call from a real-estate agent interested in seeking properties for a data center and that the Township Board had placed a moratorium, meaning no data-center applications were being accepted during the moratorium. Chairperson Galley explained that the moratorium cannot remain in place forever because data centers are legal business activity, and that the Township's role was to develop legally defensible "guardrails" and strict standards if such a development were proposed. He stated that the Planning Commission had been working on an ordinance for approximately three or four months and that other municipalities were also working on the issue. He referenced Independence Township's moratorium and said Springfield Township was farther along in the process. Commissioner Kevin Sclesky introduced Mark Marion, identified as the owner of the property that had been identified online in connection with alleged data-center plans. Mr. Marion stated that, on behalf of Rave's development, they did not know where the online rumor started and that the property had been in a development stage for approximately one or two years. He stated he has had offers to purchase but he has declined and offers. He intends to undertake their own development. He expressly stated that they had no interest in selling the property to a data center. Chairperson Galley advised that additional public questions could be raised during the public-comment period and reiterated that no data centers had been formally submitted to the Township. Old Business: 1) Sheetz Final Site Plan – 8500 Dixie Hwy – 07-36-401-011 Township Planner Megan Masson-Minock presented the final site plan for a proposed Sheetz gas station, convenience store, fast-food use, and drive-through at 8500 Dixie Highway, at the north corner of Dixie Highway and Lavon Drive, north of I-75. The proposal would demolish the existing gas station and replace it with the proposed facility. The site includes the parcel containing the existing BP station and an adjacent vacant parcel. The property is in the C-2 General Business District and Dixie Highway Overlay District. 2 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING August 25, 2026 Ms. Masson-Minock identified the Planning Commission's options as approval, approval with minor revisions/conditions, tabling, or denial. She reviewed the building placement and natural-resource protection were reported as meeting applicable standards. She explained the development spans across two parcels. The applicant had previously volunteered to combine the parcels; staff recommended that parcel combination could be made a condition because the development and infrastructure span both parcels, including a septic field and a new well. She went into parking standards; they were met except that 11 spaces were proposed to be banked: the area would remain lawn/grass and could be converted to parking if needed. There are two driveways, one on Lavon and one on Dixie Highway. The zoning ordinance limits driveway width for gas stations to 30 feet; the applicant requested 36 feet to accommodate trucks and larger vehicles. Additional pedestrian circulation requested at preliminary review was added, including a sidewalk along the west side connecting to the Dixie Highway pathway and main entrance, crosswalks connecting eastern and western parking areas to the safety path, and pedestrian access for staff to the dumpster. Planner Masson-Minock shared that the landscaping was reported as compliant, with proposed new trees and preservation of existing trees/vegetation. The ground sign includes a surrounding structure. The ordinance ordinarily limits the structure to 25% of the maximum permissible sign area; the Commission could waive that requirement. The applicant's proposed structure was approximately 64% of the permissible sign area and included stone intended to enhance the Dixie Highway Overlay. She stated that canopy and gas-station signs were compliant. Along with Building materials were reported as compliant with architectural standards. The automobile filling/convenience-station standards were generally found to be met, subject to the driveway-width request and any discretionary screening/noise buffering. Chairperson Galley acknowledged a public comment that was shared in their packet. He explained a neighboring property owner had requested an acoustical sound-dampening wall, decibel testing, and measures concerning speakers. Planner Masson-Minock explained that the Commission could impose screening and noise-buffering requirements if they felt needed. The latest plan included required teardrop lighting, stone/wood fencing, and other Dixie Highway design elements. The applicant proposed outdoor seating on the northeast side and a flagpole near the Lavon driveway as community amenities. Engineer Jason Mayer stated that an approved-as-noted engineering letter had been issued. He explained that the applicant would need permits from appropriate agencies, including the Health Department and Road Commission. Additional plan details were being added and would be completed before a preconstruction meeting. 3 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING August 25, 2026 Mr. Eric Williams of Stonefield, representing the applicant, reported that the frontage fencing had been changed from red brick to a stone color to fit in with nearby businesses. He shared comments had been added concerning no tow-truck parking and outdoor sales. He noted the applicant would seek to combine the lots and agreed to the identified requirements. He stated that Sheetz was comfortable with 40–45 surface parking spaces, that the current plan had 49 spaces, and that the 11 banked spaces could be constructed later if needed. He also stated that the applicant planned to install acorn lighting along the walkway/safety path. He requested the additional six feet of driveway width and explained that truckturning templates had been provided. He stated that there would be no high-flow diesel and that the requested driveway width was intended for delivery/fuel-delivery turning. He described the additional sign area as stone columns intended to match the Dixie Highway Overlay. The Commission generally supported the proposed 36-foot driveway width, the banked parking, the stone sign treatment, and the site plan's conformity with the Dixie Highway Overlay. Chairperson Galley and Commissioner Donato discussed the desire to avoid curb-hopping and protect landscaping, the tightness of the fuel-delivery truck route, and the fact that the proposed facility was not intended as a truck stop, service shop, or tire-repair facility. Commissioner Sclesky moved to approve the final site plan for Sheetz at 8500 Dixie Highway with conditions: - (A) combine the two lots at the earliest convenience and provide documentation to the Township; (B) permit the 11 missing parking spaces to be banked, with the Township reserving the right to require installation if determined necessary; (C) accept the proposed sign support structure as enhancing the Dixie Highway Overlay; (D) approve the requested 36-foot driveway width; and (E) resolve all engineering issues with the Township Engineer; (F) determine the Overlay District guidelines meets the standard Supported by Commissioner Hines. Vote. Yes: Galley, Hines, Sclesky, Felix, Donato, Price, No: None. Absent: Yovich. Motion approved. Immediately after the vote, a member of the public objected that the public had not been given an opportunity to see the site plan or ask questions before the motion. Chairperson Galley explained that the matter had been before the Commission the prior month. The member requested a site rendering. Chairperson Galley offered his packets site plans and materials. 2) Draft Data Center Zoning Ordinance Amendments 4 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING August 25, 2026 Planner Masson-Minock reviewed revisions and comments made after the prior Planning Commission meeting. The revised definition of data center was expanded to describe co-location, cloud computing facilities, hyperscale community facilities, cryptocurrency mining facilities, artificial-intelligence training facilities, and similar high-intensity information-technology operations. She suggested including a coolingsystem definition from the Michigan Townships Association sample ordinance. She began explained the proposed setback categories for on-site accessory data center: 100 feet from residentially used or zoned property and specified sensitive uses such as schools, medical clinics, daycare centers, preschools, hospitals and medical centers; 75 feet from other property lines. For major data center: 400 feet from the specified sensitive uses and 200 feet from all property lines. Lastly, minor data center: 100 feet from specified sensitive uses and 75 feet from all property lines. Planner Masson-Minock explained that large-scale industrial development is not allowed on a parcel within 500 feet of residentially used or zoned property and specified sensitive uses including schools, medical clinics, parks, daycare centers, preschools, hospitals and medical centers; 200 feet from other property lines. She also noted a minimum 50-foot landscape greenbelt along all property lines and minimum Screen No. 3 landscaping were proposed for data centers and large-scale industrial developments. She explained the proposed large-scale industrial provisions would control conflicting zoning provisions and would prevent an operator from avoiding thresholds by dividing operations among buildings, parcels, or phases. Planner Masson-Minock shared details regarding lighting that would cross-reference existing strict township lighting standards. The draft used 0.1 foot-candles; the MTA model ordinance could support a zero-foot-candle standard. A post-construction noise study would be required in addition to the preconstruction baseline study, with periodic testing discussed as occurring every three years. Also, Environmental-permit requirements would cross-reference existing Section 40-890 requirements rather than duplicate them. She noted the waiver for secondary containment of fuel containers was removed but additional fireprotection requirements were added. Thermal monitoring for battery-energy-storage systems and noise requirements for transformers and substations were added. Annual reporting would be required to break water use into process water, cooling water, domestic water, and irrigation water. There also was an independent, industry-recognized third-party impact analysis added. Planner Masson-Minock went into environmental-performance requirements that would address ecosystems, air quality, soil quality, and biodiversity. The performance guarantee for decommissioning and site restoration was increased to 150% of the estimated cost, certified by a third party and updated 5 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING August 25, 2026 every five years. The guarantee would run with the land, and the Township could use it for required work, with additional costs potentially recoverable from the owner/operator through taxing authority. Planner Masson-Minock explained that the Michigan Townships Association (MTA) is the professional association for Michigan townships and provides guidance and sample ordinances. She noted that the MTA cautions municipalities against adopting a sample ordinance without tailoring it to local conditions and needs. She explained the draft would be reviewed by the Township Attorney and ultimately acted upon by the Township Board if amendments were recommended. Chairperson Galley explained next steps and that the current discussion was not a vote. He explained after the Commission develops a proposal, a public hearing would be held, followed by a recommendation to the Township Board. The Township Board would have at least two readings and could return a section to the Planning Commission. Chairperson Galley asked whether one standard could be applied to all data centers or whether different size/power tiers were necessary. Planner Masson-Minock explained that the categories relate to anticipated impacts: larger facilities generally use more energy and water and generate more heat and vibration and are more difficult to remove. Commissioners discussed the MTA model's small-scale accessory-use exemption and whether the Township's categories should instead place all data centers under one set of standards, with distinctions primarily for setbacks and impacts. The discussion continued on whether the large-scale industrial provisions should remain separate from data-center provisions. Concerns were raised that combining the concepts throughout the ordinance could create confusion, particularly around electrical thresholds and terminology. Planner Masson-Minock stated that both concepts could be considered at the same time because many standards would be similar. She shared examples of possible large-scale industrial uses other than hyperscale data centers included large battery-energy-storage facilities, combinations of renewable energy and storage, power plants, and other future high-consumption uses. Commissioner Felix asked about water use and whether cooling types could be specified. Planner Masson-Minock stated that the draft already contained closed-loop cooling that would not routinely discharge to surface waters or a municipal sewer system. Alternatives could be permitted if demonstrated to have less impact. A municipal-water requirement was also discussed as an option, although Springfield Township does not have a planned municipal water expansion identified in the discussion. 6 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING August 25, 2026 Commissioner Felix expressed support for closed-loop cooling or an alternative system that is less impactful, recognizing future technology. Commissioner Donato stated that closed-loop terminology is broad enough to cover refrigerant, water, or glycol systems and discussed the implications for cooling towers and drift eliminators. Commissioner Sclesky emphasized legal defensibility and cautioned against adding unnecessary layers of language. He reported that he and Commissioner Price had reviewed other strong ordinances, including one associated with a community near Ann Arbor, and that comparison information had been provided to the commissioners that night. Commissioner Sclesky referenced legal disputes involving data-center moratoria in other Michigan communities. Planner Masson-Minock clarified that, regarding Saline Township, rejected a proposal, the developer sued, and the township settled; she did not know whether a particular review board was a factor in that settlement. The Commission discussed whether a small subcommittee would be useful to produce a clean draft. Planner Masson-Minock stated that a subcommittee or small group could be effective and suggested no more than three people. Chairperson Galley said he would follow up and send an email seeking volunteers and possible meeting times. Commissioner Hines suggested reviewing the Township's general noise and vibration ordinance rather than creating duplicative data-center-only standards. Planner Masson-Minock agreed that the subcommittee could review the existing noise section and consider whether a separate vibration provision was appropriate. Commissioner Price identified noise as a major concern, along with water. He requested more detail regarding ongoing and surprise testing, testing frequency, who performs testing, strict limits, and treatment of low-frequency noise. He also asked that the ordinance specify what happens if testing fails. Chairperson Galley stated that the Township's proposal was more stringent than the cited Sio ordinance on noise by 5 dB. No action was taken on the data-center ordinance at this meeting, and the discussion was for continued drafting and review. New Business: 7 Minutes of PLANNING COMMISSION REGULAR MEETING August 25, 2026 1) Clawson Tank Storage Preliminary Site Plan – 4634 Clawson Tank Dr – 07-36-401-011 Chairperson Galley began the first new business item which is a preliminary site plan for 4634 Clawson Tank Drive Mr. Jim Eppink, land planner and landscape architect, introduced the applicant team, including Mr. Brent DeClark, Mr. Micah Marley, Mr. Pat McWilliams of Kieft Engineering, and Mr. Jay Noonan, project architect. Mr. Eppink described an approximately eight-acre M-1 Light Industrial site on Clawson Tank Drive, south of … He further noted that the Township Board had acted decisively in adopting a moratorium to study and revise the Township's zoning standards for data centers. A member of the public interrupted to ask why the Pledge of Allegiance had not … such as mezzanines, bathrooms, kitchenettes, floor drains, and related systems. Fuel and battery storage in vehicles were discussed. Commissioner Felix noted that Section 40-630 appeared to require fuel to be drained and batteries removed … Hines, Sclesky, Felix, Donato, Price, No: None. Absent: Yovich. Motion approved. 2) Zoning Ordinance Amendments a. Draft Zoning Ordinance Amendments for Accessory Buildings and Structures and Uses Planner Masson-Minock presented amendments

text: TYRONE TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION WORKSHOP AGENDA September 23, 2026, 6:00 PM CALL TO ORDER: PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE: APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA: CALL TO THE PUBLIC: NEW BUSINESS: OLD BUSINESS: 1. Data Centers CALL TO THE PUBLIC: MISCELLANEOUS BUSINESS: ADJOURNMENT: Memorandum Ross Nicholson TO: Director of Planning & Zoning FROM: Mario A. Ortega, AICP SUBJECT: Data Center Zoning and Licensing Ordinance Amendments – Revised Draft DATE: September 17, 2026 Please find attached a revised draft of zoning ordinance amendments for data centers based upon comments from the August 26, 2026, meeting. These revisions include: • • • • Class B Definition – The addition of language to specify that whether a data center offers services to one business or multiple businesses, it will still be defined as a Class B facility. Accessory and Class A Standards – The power levels have been edited to reflect the power levels noted in the new Class definitions. The maximum sound level text now reflects using the C-weighted decibel measurement standard. Class C Landscape Standards – Added text to require that no plant species shall exceed more than 30% of the total tree or shrub or perennial provided. Class C Sound Standards – Added text to utilize the C-weighted decibel measurement standard. The licensing ordinance has been revised to reflect comments from the August 26th and September 8th meetings. These revisions include: • • • Report on Past Year Compliance – Section 6.D(3) now requires all annual reports to include language on any past year compliance issues as well as indicating if they have met any approval conditions from the previous year. Updated Bond – Section 6.D(3)(h) has been added requiring the applicant to update the bond amount based on any increase in costs. Appeals Process – The normal process for an appeal is typically to the Township Board for a license or permit, but since the Board is the issuing authority, it isn’t clear what additional review relief an applicant would have at the local level. Given that the Zoning Board of Appeals authority is from the Michigan Zoning Enabling Act, I am not sure they have the authority to conduct a general ordinance appeal. Consultation with the Township attorney would be best at this time. We look forward to your feedback as well as future feedback from the Township attorney. DRAFT DATA CENTERS ZONING ORDINANCE AMENDMENTS TYRONE TOWNSHIP, LIVINGSTON COUNTY, MICHIGAN Original text is in normal text. Text proposed for removal is in red strikethrough. Proposed text is in underlined blue text. Removed and Proposed text based on 08-26-2026 Planning Commission comments in highlight. The following amendment language is proposed to regulate data centers within the Township. This revised draft is reflective of the conversations held by the Planning Commission in the past months. SECTION 2.05 DATA CENTERS DEFINITIONS DATA CENTER. A facility designed for storage, processing, and transmission of digital data. A data center typically houses servers, hard drives, networking equipment, and other components related to digital data operations. Data center infrastructure may also include air handling equipment, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, and other related support equipment. For the purposes of this ordinance, the following classifications of data centers have been identified: A. ACCESSORY DATA CENTER. An accessory data center is a data center facility that supports a single business or organization. Accessory data centers are custom built to be supportive of the business or organization’s primary business function, operation, activities and processes. Computing by the data center is not the primary tool or function of the business and is not used to provide computing services to the business’s customers. Accessory data centers occupy less floor area than all other business related activities within a building and typically operate on less than 150 kW of power. B. CLASS A DATA CENTER. Class A data centers are small data centers built near the people or business they are intended to serve, providing real-time data processing, analysis, and action, making low-latency communication with smart devices possible. Class A data centers typically operate up to a maximum of 1 MW of power. C. CLASS B DATA CENTER. A Class B data center offers data center space to a single business or multiple businesses that want to host their computing hardware and servers offsite. These facilities provide the proper components—power, cooling, securing, and networking components—needed to do so. Companies that don’t have the space for their own data center, or an IT team dedicated to manage it, often choose a Class B data center to provide this service. A Class B data center typically operates from more than 1 MW up to 60 MW of power. D. CLASS C DATA CENTER. A Class C data center is one that typically occupies one or more warehouse-sized buildings, and houses thousands of servers to handle very large processing workloads. A Class C data center typically operates on more than 60 MW of power. Zoning Ordinance Amendments for Data Centers – REVISED Tyrone Township September 17, 2026 Page 1 ARTICLE 16A PIRO PLANNED INDUSTRIAL, RESEARCH, AND OFFICE DISTRICT SECTION 16A.02 TABLE OF PERMITTED AND SPECIAL LAND USES The following “Table of Permitted and Special Land Uses in the PIRO District” designates the land uses permitted in each of the sub-districts. A. Permitted Uses. All uses listed in the following and signified with a letter “P” shall be uses permitted by right in the corresponding PIRO sub-district B. Special Land Uses. All uses listed in the following “Table of Permitted and Special Land Uses in the PIRO District” and signified with a letter “S” shall be permitted special land uses in the corresponding sub-district, subject to review and approval of the Planning Commission in accordance with the standards and procedures of Article 23. C. Uses Not Permitted. Uses not permitted in a particular sub-district are designated with the letters “NP”. D. Accessory Uses. Buildings, structures, and uses customarily accessory to any permitted or special land use shall be permitted as approved during site plan review, in accordance with Section 21.02. E. Summary Table of Permitted and Special Land Uses in the PIRO District. The table below lists uses permitted as follows: “P” = Permitted Use; “S” = Special Land Use; and “NP” = Use Not Permitted. Uses High technology service uses including computer information transfer, communication, distribution, management, processing, administrative, laboratory, experimental, developmental, technical, or testing services. Data processing / computer centers, including service and maintenance of electronic data processing equipment and software development Accessory Data Center Class A Data Center Class B Data Center Class C Data Center PIRO-A Research and Office * PIRO-B Light Industry** PIRO-C General Industry*** P P S P P P S S NP NP NP NP S NP NP NP NP NP * Outdoor storage and display of goods and materials is prohibited. ** Outdoor storage and display of goods and materials requires special land use approval. *** Outdoor storage and display of goods and materials is permitted. Zoning Ordinance Amendments for Data Centers – REVISED Tyrone Township September 17, 2026 Page 2 ARTICLE 22 SPECIAL LAND USES SECTION 22.05 SITE DESIGN CONDITIONS All special land uses shall comply with the site plan design requirements of Article 23. In addition, certain special land uses shall also comply with design conditions unique to that use. Those special land uses and conditions are listed herein. W. Data Centers 1. Purpose. The purpose of the following standards is to establish regulations for the design, placement, and operation of data centers within the Township. Data centers have high energy and cooling needs, can generate noise that may be heard off-site, have high security needs, and have special building features that create land use impacts that must be managed. The regulations in this subsection are intended to: a. Ensure compatibility with surrounding land uses. b. Manage land use impacts, including but not limited to noise, water usage, hazardous materials use, lighting, and energy usage. c. Protect public health, safety, and welfare. 2. Accessory and Class A Data Centers Accessory and Class A data centers that are designed to serve the needs of a specific business or organization are permitted subject to the following regulations: a. Special Land Use and Site Plan Review and Approval Required. Accessory and Class A data centers that have an energy draw of under 150 kW up to 1 MW shall be required to obtain special land use approval pursuant to Article 22 and site plan approval, pursuant to Article 23. b. Minimum Setbacks. Accessory and Class A data centers shall comply with the setback requirements for the zoning district in which they are located. c. Maximum Sound Pressure Level. The audible sound from an accessory and Class A data center shall not exceed 45 dB A a C-weighted decibel level of 45 dB(C), measured at the property line closest to the data center. The facility shall comply with all noise requirements of Section 21.16 with the exception that all measurements shall be for C-weighted decibel levels and that the maximum sound levels of Section 21.16, Table 2 shall be 45 dB(C). d. Code Requirements. Accessory and Class A data centers shall comply with all state construction and electrical codes and Township building code requirements. e. Energy Usage. Accessory data centers shall utilize no more than 150 kW of power. Class A data centers shall utilize no more than 1 MW of power. 3. Class B Data Centers. Class B data centers shall be permitted subject to the following regulations: a. Special Land Use and Site Plan Review and Approval Required. Class B data centers shall be required to obtain special land use approval pursuant to Article 22 and site plan approval, pursuant to Article 23. b. Submittal Requirements. Class B data centers shall comply with applicable site plan data requirements in Section 23.02. In addition, the following documentation shall be submitted to demonstrate compliance with requirements herein: Zoning Ordinance Amendments for Data Centers – REVISED Tyrone Township September 17, 2026 Page 3 i. Natural Feature Preservation. The data center site plan shall include a tree survey and plan for cutting of trees greater than eight (8) inches measured 48 inches above grade. No such trees shall be cut in any required setback other than those reasonably required for the installation of a drive to access the facility. Retention of natural grades, soils, and groundcover material is encouraged where feasible. The treatment of existing plant material will comply with the requirements of Section 21A.08. ii. Environmental Impact Analysis. An analysis by a qualified professional third-party, approved by the Township, shall be required to identify and assess any potential impacts on the natural environment including, but not limited to, wetlands and other fragile ecosystems, historical and cultural sites, and antiquities. The applicant shall take appropriate measures to minimize, eliminate, or mitigate adverse impacts identified in the analysis. An applicant shall identify and evaluate the significance of any net effects or concerns that will remain after mitigation efforts. The applicant shall comply with applicable parts of the following: Michigan Natural Resources and Environmental Protection Act (Act 451 of 1994, MCL 324.101 et seq.) including but not limited to: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. Part 31 Water Resources Protection (MCL seq.), Part 91 Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control (MCL 324.9101 et seq.), Part 301 Inland Lakes and Streams (MCL 324.30101 et seq.), Part 303 Wetlands (MCL 324.30301 et seq.), Part 323 Shoreland Protection and Management (MCL 324.32301 et seq.), Part 325 Great Lakes Submerged Lands (MCL 324.32501 et seq.), Part 353 Sand Dunes Protection and Management (MCL 324.35301 et seq.). The applicant also must conduct a Phase I environmental site assessment and, if risks are identified, a Phase II environmental site assessment. A copy of the reports must be submitted to the Township. If remediation or cleanup is indicated, the applicant also must conduct a Phase III environmental site assessment and provide a copy of the report to the Township. iii. Stormwater Management Plan. Data centers shall not increase stormwater runoff onto adjacent properties. The application shall include a stormwater management plan prepared by a registered civil engineer showing how stormwater runoff shall be managed and demonstrating that runoff from the site shall not exceed the agricultural runoff rate or otherwise cause undue flood. The plan shall show how the facility complies with all state, county and local stormwater management requirements. Any necessary permits from outside agencies for off-site discharge shall be provided. It should also be demonstrated that maintenance procedures and products will not introduce chemicals or create detrimental impacts to the natural environment, groundwater, and wildlife. iv. Stormwater Infiltration Study. An analysis by a qualified professional third- party, approved by the Township, shall be required to account for the proposed layout of the data center facility and how the proposed facility or site improvements placement affects stormwater infiltration, including calculations for a 100-year rain- event (storm). Percolation tests or site-specific soil information shall be provided to demonstrate infiltration on-site without the use of engineered solutions. v. Decommissioning Plan. A decommissioning and land reclamation plan shall be prepared and submitted, pursuant to subsection 3(c)(xii), herein. vi. Wildlife Impact Analysis. An analysis by a qualified professional third-party, approved by the Township, to identify and assess any potential impacts on wildlife and endangered species. The applicant shall take appropriate measures to minimize, eliminate, or mitigate adverse impacts identified in the analysis. The applicant shall identify and evaluate the significance of any net effects or concerns that will remain after mitigation efforts. Sites requiring special scrutiny include wildlife refuges, other areas where birds are highly concentrated, bat hibernacula, wooded ridge Zoning Ordinance Amendments for Data Centers – REVISED Tyrone Township September 17, 2026 Page 4 tops that attract wildlife, sites that are frequented by federally or state listed endangered species of birds and bats, significant bird migration pathways, and areas that have landscape features known to attract large numbers of raptors. At a minimum, the analysis shall include a thorough review of existing information regarding species and potential habitats in the vicinity of the project area. Where appropriate, surveys for bats, raptors, or general avian use should be conducted. The analysis shall include the potential effects on species listed under the federal Endangered Species Act and Michigan’s Endangered Species Protection Law. The applicant shall follow all pre-construction and post-construction recommendations of the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. The analysis shall indicate whether a post-construction wildlife mortality study will be conducted and, if not, the reasons why such a study does not need to be conducted. Power lines should be placed underground, when feasible, to prevent avian collisions and electrocutions. All aboveground lines, transformers, or conductors should follow any Avian Power Line Interaction Committee (APLIC, http://www.aplic.org/) guidelines to prevent avian mortality. vii. Fire and Public Safety Protection Plan. A fire protection plan, which identifies the fire risks associated with the data center that describes the fire suppression system that will be implemented; describes what measures will be used to reduce the risk of fires re-igniting (i.e., implementing a “fire watch”); identifies the water sources that will be available for the local fire department; identifies a system for continuous monitoring, early detection sensors, and appropriate venting; and explains all other measures that will be implemented to prevent, detect, control, and suppress fires and explosions. It will be the burden of the applicant to ensure said procedures and protocols provided to the various emergency service departments is the most up to date version. Any data center that includes battery storage or other devices capable of storing energy shall demonstrate compliance with National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) Standard 855, Installation of Stationary Energy Storage Systems, or any applicable successor standard. Battery storage facilities shall comply with applicable requirements in Section 22.05.U. viii. Hazardous Materials and Waste Plan. A hazardous materials and waste plan shall be prepared and submitted by the applicant. The plan shall describe the nature of storage and processing of hazardous materials and waste, and shall contain the following elements: 1. The name, quantity, and location of all hazardous materials to be stored or used in the facility. 2. Identification of all required state and federal permits related to the handling of the hazardous materials and hazardous waste. Copies of all permits shall be provided to the Township prior to beginning operation. 3. Proposed procedures in the event that hazardous materials or hazardous wastes are released and have the potential to cause harm to people, property, or the environment. 4. Method of disposing of hazardous waste. 5. Protocol for notifying the Township in the event of a hazardous materials or hazardous waste spill or release. ix. Sound and Vibration Modeling Analysis. A predictive sound and vibration modeling analysis, prepared by a qualified acoustician or sound engineer, shall be submitted. The analysis shall demonstrate compliance with the sound and vibration requirements set forth in subsection 3(c)(iv), herein. The analysis shall factor in all equipment that may be utilized in the cooling of the facility. x. Water Usage Plan. A water usage plan shall be prepared and submitted, pursuant to subsection 4(c)(vii), herein. Zoning Ordinance Amendments for Data Centers – REVISED Tyrone Township September 17, 2026 Page 5 xi. Electrical Grid Feasibility and Power Utilization Plan. An electrical grid feasibility and power utilization Plan shall be prepared and submitted for review. The plan shall provide a detailed analysis of the lifetime need of electrical power for the data center, the capability of the existing components of the electrical grid to provide the necessary power, detailed identification of any necessary improvements anywhere between the power generation facility and the data center facility in order to meet the data center’s needs and a legally binding agreement from the applicant that any and the cost of any and all improvements necessary to provide the power needs of the data center shall be provided by the applicant, the operator and any successor operator for the lifetime of the facility. xii. Operations Plan. An operations plan shall be submitted, which shall describe the essential functions of the facility, the inspection protocol, emergency procedures, and safety standards. The plan shall also identify operator names and provide contact information. xiii. Traffic Impact Analysis. A traffic impact analysis shall be prepared for the construction and operation phases, which shall be based on accepted engineering standards and methods established by the Institute of Transportation Engineers, Michigan Department of Transportation, and/or Livingston County Road Department. The traffic impact analysis shall address, at a minimum, the following considerations: estimated 24-hour and peak hour traffic prior to and after

WHITE LAKE TOWNSHIP ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS Applicant: Matthew Cottrell Owners: Matthew Cottrell and Gina Wlodarski Address: 10400 Cedar Island Road, White Lake, Michigan 48386 Parcel Number: 12-27-454-006 Zoning: R1-C, Single Family Residential Request Summary: Substandard Lot Review to permit reconstruction of the existing garage and construction of an attached residential addition with an approximately 6-foot west side-yard setback, where an 8-foot setback is otherwise permitted for the substandard lot. Meeting Date: September 24, 2026 Attachments: Application and Survey Project Description The subject property is a lakefront parcel located at 10400 Cedar Island Road and zoned R1-C, Single Family Residential. Township assessing records identify the property as Lot 36 of Cedar View No. 1, approximately 0.272 acres in area, and improved with a 936-square-foot ranch dwelling and a 440square-foot detached garage, both identified as having been constructed in 1957. The applicant proposes to reconstruct the existing garage and construct an addition connecting the garage to the dwelling. According to the application, the existing garage was constructed within a utility easement and has experienced floor failure that created safety concerns. The replacement garage would be narrowed to avoid the easement, while the proposed addition would connect the reconstructed garage to the residence and improve access between the house and the water. 8 Item A. The property is considered a substandard lot because it does not meet the current minimum lot-width requirement of the R1-C district. The Building Official determined that the applicable side-yard setback may be reduced from 10 feet to 8 feet by right due to the lot’s substandard width. The proposed reconstructed garage and attached addition would maintain an approximately 6-foot west side-yard setback, requiring an additional 2 feet of relief through the Substandard Lot Review process. Site History The property is Lot 36 of Cedar View No. 1, a subdivision approved in 1957. The lot has remained in the same general configuration since the subdivision was created. Township assessing records show that the existing house and detached garage were also constructed in 1957. The current legal description continues to identify the property as Lot 36 of Cedar View No. 1, and the assessing records do not identify a later split or combination. The lot’s substandard width and existing development pattern are therefore longstanding conditions rather than the result of a recent land division. Substandard Lot Review Standards: Sec 7.27 Nonconforming Lots of Record 1. The lot was legally established pursuant to all applicable provisions of Michigan law or White Lake Township ordinance. Staff Comment: The subject property is Lot 36 of Cedar View No. 1, which was platted and approved in 1957. The current legal description continues to identify the property as Lot 36, and Township assessing records do not identify a later split or combination. The lot’s substandard width is therefore a longstanding condition associated with the original subdivision rather than the result of a recent land division. Staff Finding: This standard is met. 9 Item A. 2. The construction that will result from the issuance of said permits will be in keeping with the general character of the neighborhood in which the construction will take place. Staff Comment: The property would remain in single-family residential use. The proposal involves reconstruction of the existing garage and construction of an addition connecting the garage to the existing dwelling. The work would remain residential in character and would not introduce a new use or building type inconsistent with the surrounding lakefront neighborhood. The replacement garage would also be narrower than the existing garage in order to move the structure away from the existing utility easement. Staff Finding: This standard is met. 3. The proposed use will not have a significant effect on adjoining and nearby property owners. Staff Comment: The property would remain in single-family residential use, and the proposed improvements would not increase residential density or introduce additional traffic, parking demand, or activity beyond that normally associated with a single-family dwelling. Although the reconstructed garage and attached addition would be located approximately six feet from the west property line, the proposal maintains approximately six feet of separation from the adjoining property line and exceeds the absolute five-foot minimum side-yard setback established by Section 7.27(B)(vii). Compliance with applicable building, drainage, and other permitting requirements will remain necessary. Staff Finding: This standard is met. 4. The design of the proposed structure is appropriate for the area, width, and shape of the lot, and is designed in such a fashion as to provide adequate access for fire and other emergency vehicles. Staff Comment: The proposed design responds to the limited width of the lot and the location of the existing utility easement. According to the applicant, the existing garage extends into the easement. The proposed garage would be reconstructed at a narrower width, allowing it to be moved away from the easement while maintaining a functional garage and providing an attached connection to the residence. 10 Item A. The submitted site plan maintains approximately six feet between the proposed construction and the west property line, which remains greater than the five-foot minimum established for emergency access and fire separation. Vehicular access from Cedar Island Road would remain available. Staff Finding: This standard is met. 5. The proposed design is consistent with the extent to which other developed lots in the subdivision have maintained the setbacks and other required provisions of this Ordinance. Staff Comment: Cedar View No. 1 was platted in 1957 with a series of relatively narrow residential lots along Cedar Island Road and the water. The subject lot and surrounding properties were developed within this original subdivision pattern. The proposed design responds to these existing dimensional limitations by reconstructing the garage at a narrower width and maintaining approximately six feet from the west property line. While this is less than the otherwise applicable reduced side-yard setback, it remains above the absolute five-foot minimum required for a substandard-lot approval. Staff Finding: This standard is met. 6. The nonconforming lot shall meet all other requirements of this Ordinance, which requirements for the purpose of this Section shall be deemed to include reasonable provisions for automobile parking. Staff Comment: The property would continue to provide off-street parking

Site Type Change August 26, 2026 A “site type” identifies allowed land uses per use group. Land uses are categorized into “use groups” that are similar in intensity or uses that are typically clustered together in a traditional community. We have included a description of the “site types” available for the Town Center zoning district below, as well as the “use groups” allowed by each site type. Following this is a table listing the land uses included in each use group. Site Type A site type for a particular parcel is determined by a number of factors, including size, access, length of frontage, location, and context. Descriptions of each possible site type are provided below: A. Site Type A: Site Type A is composed of lots one-half (0.5) acre or smaller and is reserved primarily for residential use and for smaller non-residential use which is compatible with a residential setting. Site Type A is generally located in areas which serve as a transition between the street and neighboring residential areas. Site Type A lots are typically mid-block and not located on a corner. The building form selected for these sites must consider both the front elevation that fronts on the street but also the rear/side elevation that is adjacent to residential in order to maintain compatibility with adjacent uses. These sites are intended for small sized neighborhood residential, commercial/office, or mixed-use sites. B. Site Type B: Made up mostly of lots mostly between one-half (0.5) and one (1) acre in area, the Site Type B category may include free standing single-use sites developed for residential, commercial, and office uses serving the surrounding neighborhood or mixed-use developments. Size and character may vary based on the unique characteristic of each parcel. Small retail and food service uses would often be found in this category, as well as small single or multi-tenant commercial or office buildings. C. Site Type C: The sites in Site Type C are mostly larger than one (1) acre in area. Site Type C size and character may vary based on the unique characteristic of each parcel. This category can include free-standing single-use or mixed-use developments that are designed to serve a broader community-wide market. These sites are intended for community commercial/office, multiple family residential, and mixed-use sites. D. Site Type D: The sites in Site Type D are very large sites are generally two (2) acres or greater in area. Site Type D size and character may vary based on the unique characteristic of each parcel. This category is intended for light industrial, mixed-use sites, large scale retail, and campus style developments. Site Type D are large lots with the potential for out lots of smaller building types on same parcel. Huron St. and approx. 741 feet along Kalitta Ct.). - Context: This parcel creates a possible location for a retail “node” at this street intersection, given the Aldi and future Culver’s across S. Huron St. - Proposed Site Type D: Due to its size, and location at a corner with a traffic light, Site Type D would allow/potentially allow the greatest variety of commercial uses that could be accommodated by the parcel’s characteristics. The new uses listed under use groups 5 and 6 are all Special Land Uses, which will necessitate the applicant’s proposal to meet the Special Land Use criteria in the Ordinance, and obtain Planning Commission approval after a Public Hearing. Process to Modify the Regulating Plan Sec. 502. – Applicability and Organization, of Article 5 – Form-Based Districts states the following when a change to a regulating plan is needed. Ordinance provisions are listed in italics, followed by CWA comments after each in regular text: 5. Modification of regulating plan: Specific building form, use group, and design standards applied within each regulating plan are based upon the designation of site type. Any modification of site type may be determined by the Planning Commission, notice and after conducting a public hearing in accordance with Article 18. The Planning Commission shall consider the following in making a determination to modify a site type or street type designation: A The applicant's property cannot be used for the purpose permitted in the form-based district. CWA Comment: Use groups 2, 3 and 4 are permitted in the existing site types A & B, as well as the proposed site type D. The difference in site type D is: - Single-family detached and attached residential, and two-family residential uses would no longer be allowed. Given the commercial character of this part of S. Huron St., we would consider this change to be consistent with the surrounding land uses. - Site type D would also possibly allow more commercial uses, in addition to uses that have a drive-through component if any such proposal received Special Land Use approval from the Planning Commission. Again, we think this change would be consistent with the surrounding land uses along S. Huron St., and the Township would have additional protections in place to consider any of the Special Land Uses that a site type D could propose. B. Area has been added to or deleted from the subject property in question, requiring the modification. CWA Comment: As described above, the subject site’s property was combined to create a larger parcel in 2022. This larger parcel size is consistent with the size for a site type D designation. 8 7151 Kalitta Ct. Site Type Change August 26, 2026 C. The proposed modification and resulting development will not alter the essential character of the area. CWA Comment: The proposed uses of the new 5.07-acre parcel created in 2022 are not currently known. However, as a site type D, single-family and similarly-scaled residential uses would not be permitted. Also, a site type D could possibly expand potential commercial uses as a Special Land Use proposal, after evaluation and approval by the Planning Commission. D. The proposed modification meets the intent of the district. CWA Comment: Per the Ypsilanti Township 2020 Master Plan, this site is located in the Township Core future land use category. The intent of this category is to serve as the central gathering place and commercial base of the township. Buildout will be market responsive with a variety of uses including civic, regional and local commercial, hotels and restaurants, office, multiple-family housing, and open space that will meet the daily needs of the Township residents. Given the site’s frontage on S. Huron St., that it’s a corner lot on intersection with a traffic light, and that it is close to other commercial uses, we think changing the site type to “D,” which potentially allows for a greater diversity of commercial uses, meets the intent of this district. E. Existing streets have been improved and/or new streets constructed that may result in the modification of a specific site type. CWA Comment: Kalitta Ct. was built within the last five years. Kalitta Ct. gives the site access to S. Huron St. via a new traffic light. Given these new facilities, it is our opinion that this location could accommodate the traffic generated by the uses allowed/potentially allowed on a site type D property. F. Modification to the Regulating Plan is in conformance to the Master Plan and Placemaking Plan. CWA Comment: See our comments under “D” above. RECOMMENDATIONS We recommend approving the proposed change to the Town Center Regulating Plan, changing the site type for the subject property from A & B to D. We base this recommendation on the site’s characteristics of size (5.07 acres), having road frontage on both S. Huron St. and Kalitta Ct., that this intersection is controlled by a traffic light. The Town Center is intended to be the commercial core of the Township, and this site type change could help realize this goal. Therefore, we think the proposal meets the criteria to modify the Town Center Regulating Plan. In addition, the new land uses listed for a site type D are all Special Land Uses.
